prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Mastercard Inc" (ticker MA), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "MA", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Mastercard Incorporated
result.industry: Electronic payments network and payment services
markets: Card payment network (credit, debit, prepaid, commercial) and cross-border payments
Value-added services: cyber security, fraud and identity, data analytics, consulting, loyalty
Open banking, account-to-account and real-time payments
Digital wallets, tokenization, agentic commerce and stablecoin/crypto payments

mission.plain: Make paying and getting paid safe, simple and available to everyone, everywhere, in a digital economy.

about.plain: Mastercard runs the network that carries card payments between shoppers' banks and shops' banks. When you tap a Mastercard, its computers check the payment, help spot fraud and tell both banks to move the money, in about a second. It does not lend money itself; it charges small fees on each payment. It also sells extra services such as fraud protection, data insights and cyber security.
about.customers: Banks and fintechs that issue its cards, banks that sign up shops, merchants, governments and businesses that use its services.
about.everyday: The red-and-yellow circles logo on about 3.46 billion cards and phone wallets used to pay in shops and online around the world.

money.plain: Fees for carrying and clearing card payments, especially cross-border ones ($19,476M in 2025)
Fraud and cyber security, identity, data analytics, consulting, loyalty and open banking ($13,315M in 2025, up 23%)
Bank-to-bank payments and data access tools, partly from the Finicity acquisition
Settling stablecoin payments and buying BVNK for $1.5bn plus a $300M earnout (pending, 2026)
Letting AI shopping agents pay safely with tokenized cards

result.summary: Mastercard has one of the strongest moats in business: a two-sided network of about 3.46 billion cards and tens of millions of accepting merchants that only Visa matches globally, which lets it earn a 57.6% operating margin (2025). Its brand, the security and tokenization built into the network, and switching costs for banks under long contracts reinforce this, though regulation, real-time payment systems and stablecoins are long-term threats.

pricingPower.evidence: Net revenue grew from $15,301M in 2020 to $32,791M in 2025 while gross dollar volume grew about 9% a year (2025: $10.6T, +9% local currency), showing it has been able to add services and raise fees faster than volume; Q2 2026 revenue rose 14% on 8% volume growth, though fee increases draw merchant lawsuits and regulation.

moats.evidence: Its interlocking circles logo and the 'Priceless' campaign make it one of the world's best-known brands, trusted for acceptance everywhere.

Banks sign multi-year issuing deals with incentives, and switching card portfolios between networks is costly and disruptive, but large issuers do switch at renewal (e.g. Capital One moving debit to Discover's network).
About 3.46 billion cards (June 2026) make merchants accept it, and near-universal acceptance makes banks and consumers want its cards; only Visa has comparable two-sided scale.
Processing 175.5 billion switched transactions in 2025 on largely fixed-cost infrastructure gives very low unit costs and a 57.6% operating margin.
Global card payments are effectively a duopoly with Visa outside China, and a new global network would struggle to reach the scale needed to earn a return.
It does not lend, so it carries no credit risk, unlike American Express, but this model is shared with Visa.
Decades of transaction data feed AI fraud scoring (Decision Intelligence) and tokenization that rivals find hard to match, but Visa has similar capabilities.
It has no exclusive natural resource; its transaction data set is valuable but not exclusive since Visa and banks see similar data.

customers.evidence: Issuer relationships are long-lived and renewed for years, cards in issue grew 7.2% to 3.46 billion by June 2026, and value-added services revenue grew 23% in 2025 as banks buy more from it, though merchants dislike its fees and sue over interchange.

talent.evidence: In 2026 Mastercard was named to Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For, Glassdoor's Best Places to Work (US and UK) and Forbes' Best Employers for New Grads, with about 39,800 employees at end-2025.

product.evidence: Its network is one of only two truly global card systems with near-universal acceptance, and it ranked No. 6 in Fortune's 2026 AIQ 75 list for AI use; it leads with tokenization and Click to Pay, though Visa is broadly equal.

competitors.name: Visa Inc.
competitors.note: The other global card network; competes for every issuer contract, merchant, cross-border flow and value-added service

competitors.name: American Express Company
competitors.note: Closed-loop premium card network and issuer competing for high-spend consumer and corporate volume

competitors.name: Capital One Financial Corporation (Discover Global Network)
competitors.note: Bought Discover in 2025 and is moving debit and some credit cards onto its own networks, pulling volume from Mastercard

competitors.name: China UnionPay
competitors.note: Largest card network by cards issued; dominant in China and expanding abroad

competitors.name: PayPal Holdings, Inc.
competitors.note: Digital wallet and Venmo that can route payments through bank accounts; also a Mastercard partner

competitors.name: National Payments Corporation of India (UPI)
competitors.note: Government-backed real-time payment system handling most Indian digital payments

competitors.name: Banco Central do Brasil (Pix)
competitors.note: Free instant payment system in Brazil that has taken share from debit cards

competitors.name: Fiserv, Inc.
competitors.note: Owns US debit networks (Star, Accel) competing for debit routing

competitors.name: JCB Co., Ltd.
competitors.note: Japanese card network competing mainly in Japan and Asian travel

competitors.name: Block, Inc.
competitors.note: Cash App and Square encourage bank and peer-to-peer flows that bypass cards

competitors.name: Apple Inc.
competitors.note: Apple Pay controls the wallet layer and could steer users to pay-by-bank

competitors.name: Stripe, Inc.
competitors.note: Payment processor building stablecoin and bank-payment alternatives to card rails

competitors.name: Adyen N.V.
competitors.note: Global processor that partners with networks but pushes local and account-to-account methods

competitors.name: Experian / FICO and other fraud-data firms
competitors.note: Compete with Mastercard's identity, fraud and data services

estimates.name: Capital One Financial Corporation (Discover Global Network)
Experian / FICO and other fraud-data firms

threats: US regulation and litigation: merchant interchange lawsuits and settlements, the proposed Credit Card Competition Act forcing a second network on credit cards, and EU/UK scrutiny of cross-border and scheme fees (2025 litigation provision $504M)
Government-backed real-time payment systems such as UPI (India), Pix (Brazil), FedNow and European schemes like Wero that make account-to-account payments free and instant
Stablecoins and pay-by-bank checkout from Stripe, PayPal, Apple and others that could route payments around card rails
Capital One moving Discover-network debit and credit volume off Mastercard after its 2025 Discover acquisition
AI shopping agents changing how checkout works, which could favour whoever controls the agent or wallet
Slower cross-border travel or a global downturn, since cross-border fees are among its most profitable revenue

ceo.name: Michael Miebach
ceo.background: German-born; studied business/economics at the University of Passau; former Barclays and Citibank executive; joined Mastercard in 2010, ran Middle East and Africa, then Chief Product Officer and President before becoming CEO in January 2021

c1.evidence: It is co-leader with Visa of global electronic payments, which still grows (GDV +9% in 2025 to $10.6T) as cash declines, but card payments are a maturing rather than an emerging industry.

c2.evidence: Banks and merchants choose it because nearly everyone accepts and carries it (3.46 billion cards), plus its fraud and tokenization tools; this two-sided network has been built over 60 years and is extremely hard to copy.

c3.evidence: The Mastercard logo is recognised by billions and, with Visa, it is the default way to pay by card worldwide; consumers rarely think about it but almost never avoid it.

c4.evidence: It repeatedly emphasises an inclusive, digital economy and pledged to bring 1 billion people and 50 million small businesses into the digital economy by 2025, but the core business is fee-driven payments.

c6.evidence: “Trusted, everywhere, Priceless”: most people associate it with secure, universally accepted payments and its long-running ad campaign, a mostly positive impression apart from merchants' complaints about fees.

c7.evidence: It rides the secular shift from cash to digital and online payments plus growing cyber-security and data services (VAS revenue +23% in 2025), a market measured in tens of trillions of dollars.

c8.evidence: Beyond cards it is expanding into open banking, B2B payments, account-to-account rails, stablecoins (the pending $1.5bn BVNK deal) and agentic commerce.

m1.evidence: Miebach articulates a clear multi-rail vision (cards, account-to-account, stablecoins, AI agent payments via Agent Pay), though it is an evolution of the existing network rather than a radical new future.

m2.evidence: Miebach is a professional manager, not a founder, but has spent 16 years at Mastercard and invests for the long term, e.g. in tokenization and agentic commerce.

m4.evidence: Mastercard was named to Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For in 2026 and Miebach stresses customer partnerships, but there is limited direct evidence of a servant-leadership style.

m5.evidence: The company keeps launching products (Click to Pay, Agent Pay, Decision Intelligence) and ranked No. 6 in Fortune's 2026 AIQ 75, though this culture predates Miebach under Ajay Banga.

m6.evidence: Miebach was Chief Product Officer and is closely involved in product strategy, but his background is business and banking rather than engineering.

m7.evidence: Under Miebach Mastercard has pursued financial-inclusion pledges and its Center for Inclusive Growth, and no personal scandals are known, though the company also faces antitrust and fee lawsuits.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Michael Miebach giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Miebach has a conventional, low-key corporate style and is not a widely known public personality.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in 2021, net revenue rose from $18,884M (2021) to $32,791M (2025) and diluted EPS from $8.76 to $16.52, with Q2 2026 revenue up 14%.

m10.evidence: Mastercard is not known for frugality; operating expenses rose to $13,894M in 2025 and it spends heavily on marketing and sponsorships.

c10.evidence: Its network lets billions of people in over 200 countries and territories pay safely by card, phone or online, and its fraud tools protect them, improving everyday commerce worldwide.

p2.evidence: Running a global network that processed 175.5 billion switched transactions in 2025 securely and almost without downtime is very hard and central to the world economy.

f2.evidence: Operating margin rose from 52.8% in 2020 to 57.6% in 2025 (with a small dip to 55.3% in 2024); it reports no gross margin.

f3.evidence: Debt of $24.6B at June 2026 exceeds cash of $11.3B and equity is small ($7,746M at end-2025) because of buybacks, but debt is under 1.5 times 2025 operating cash flow of $17,648M.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose every year from $8,081M (2020) to $18,897M (2025), and operating cash flow rose from $11,980M (2023) to $14,780M (2024) and $17,648M (2025).

v1.evidence: Its network is accepted almost everywhere and as safe as any, but Visa offers essentially the same thing, so it is co-best rather than clearly best.

v2.evidence: In 2026 it was named to Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For, Glassdoor's Best Places to Work (US and UK) and Forbes' America's Best Employers for New Grads.

c5.evidence: If it vanished overnight, hundreds of millions of cardholders and millions of merchants would lose a way to pay, especially across borders and online, until Visa and local systems absorbed the volume.
